Q577890.summary: Scratched into the plaster of a room on the Palatine Hill, a crude figure with the head of a donkey hangs on a cross, while a young man raises his hand toward it; the Greek caption reads, roughly, 'Alexamenos worships [his] god'. It was made to mock a Christian, perhaps a page boy in the imperial household. Yet this scorn is often called the oldest surviving image of Jesus, and it is the earliest known picture of the crucifixion: before Christians themselves dared to depict the cross, a scoffer drew it — and in doing so bore witness to the faith he ridiculed.
facts: It was discovered in 1857 in the domus Gelotiana, a building on the Palatine that served as a school (paedagogium) for imperial page boys, and was later cut from the wall for preservation.
In a neighbouring room a different hand wrote 'ALEXAMENOS FIDELIS' — 'Alexamenos is faithful' — perhaps a friend's reply, or Alexamenos's own.
Early Christian writers, among them Tertullian and Minucius Felix, record the slander that Christians worshipped a donkey's head; this graffito is that slander in pictures.
Its date is debated, with proposals from the late 1st to the late 3rd century; around AD 200 is most widely accepted.
Q577890.notes: A hostile caricature, not a devotional image; it stays in the collection as a witness to how Christ was first pictured. Dating is disputed (late 1st to late 3rd century proposed); c. 200 is the consensus and matches the featured Journey entry, so the sort year 200 keeps it in the 2nd century. A minority view (I. Soon) reads it as Christian self-parody. Photographs: Justin Benttinen, 2023, Palatine Museum (CC BY-SA 4.0); the high-contrast version is shown because the scratches are faint in natural light.

Q60761471.summary: Around this ivory cylinder runs a continuous frieze of haloed figures seated on high-backed, cushioned chairs: Christ as Pantokrator, the apostles and the Virgin. The figures are carved in deep relief with softly falling drapery, and the tapered lip at the top was made to receive a lid that is now lost. It is a rare survival among Middle Byzantine ivory boxes.
facts: Cleveland describes it as the only known pyx to survive from the Middle Byzantine period (c. 843–1204).
On grounds of style it is attributed to the 'Triptych Group', a workshop of ivory carvers active in Constantinople between about 950 and 1010.
Q60761471.notes: CMA 1973.4. Cleveland qualifies the Triptych Group attribution as 'probably by'.

cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-smyrna.summary: Christ, standing full-length and haloed, raises his hand in speech toward John, who stretches out his hands to receive the message; below, an angel stands before the walled buildings of the city of Smyrna. The simple drawing captures the dialogue of the Revelation's letters to the churches.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.

cur:monumental-san-clemente-anastasis.summary: Christ, haloed and robed in gold, strides to the right carrying a cross-staff, grasping Adam by the wrist to draw him up from the underworld; a demon below clutches at Adam's foot, and at the left a smaller figure with a square halo, the living donor, appears beside a jewelled book. Despite its damage, the painting conveys with great force Christ's victory over death.
facts: Apart from Santa Maria Antiqua, the lower basilica of San Clemente holds the largest collection of early medieval wall paintings in Rome; the church was buried beneath the new basilica built around 1099–1120.
Restorations of the church were undertaken in the 9th century, the period to which this painting is generally assigned.
cur:monumental-san-clemente-anastasis.notes: Commons descriptions call it 'Christ in Purgatory'; the iconography is that of the Anastasis (Descent into Limbo). The donor with the square halo is often identified as Pope Leo IV (847–855), but this is not confirmed here.
